name: Cappadocian Greek

ancestors.notes: Modern Greek dialect group descended from Medieval Greek, formerly spoken in Cappadocia (central Anatolia) until the 1923 Greek-Turkish population exchange (Wikipedia: Cappadocian Greek).

"Among all Greek dialects, Cappadocian Greek is the one most influenced by Turkish": Turkish vowel harmony, SOV word-order tendencies, and phonemes not native to Greek — ı, ö, ü, š, ž, tš, dž (Wikipedia: Cappadocian Greek; Dawkins 1916 as cited there).

notes: Cappadocian Greek (Kapadokika), a critically endangered Modern Greek dialect group (~2,800 speakers, UNESCO 2015 figure) formerly spoken across Cappadocia, central Turkey; speakers were resettled in Central/Northern Greece after the 1923 population exchange. Documented in the Greek alphabet for modern purposes, so the base grapheme inventory is inherited from Modern Greek (`el`) unchanged. Turkish contact introduced phonemes absent from, or marginal in, standard Greek — /ɯ/ (ı), /ø/ (ö), /y/ (ü), /ʃ ʒ tʃ dʒ/ (š ž tš dž per Dawkins' transcription) — but no confirmed native Greek-alphabet spelling convention for these sounds could be sourced this session, so they are left unmapped rather than fabricated; a future revision with access to Dawkins (1916) 'Modern Greek in Asia Minor' or Janse's Cappadocian corpus could add them as graphemes/allophones. Turkish is wired as an adstrate per the cited descent, at a higher weight than the more modest Ottoman-period adstrate on `el` itself, reflecting Cappadocian's exceptionally deep Turkish contact.

location.notes: Central Anatolia (Cappadocia), the region spoken in before the 1923 population exchange.
